newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - June 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - June 16.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- FABIANS URGE LABOUR TO BACK SERVICE SECTOR

The Fabian Society, the socialist group, has appealed to the new Labour government to adopt a more positive approach towards the service sector, particularly retailing. Urging the government to abandon its traditional concern with industry, the society argues that the interests of the consumer should be given a higher priority in policy-making. The group also calls for the deregulation of postal services, government support for out-of- town shopping centres, and the creation of a genuine European single market in retailing.
-- REGISTRARS FACE OFT PROBE

The Office of Fair Trading is to investigate allegations that Lloyds Bank, Royal Bank of Scotland and Independent Registrars Group -- the three main share registrars in the UK -- are depriving investors using nominee companies of the right to vote at meetings or receive annual reports and shareholder perks. The claim has been made by Apcims, the body representing private client stockbrokers.
-- SHARELINK OVERWHELMED

Telephone stockbroker ShareLink was forced to close its telephone lines to new customers on several occasions over the past two weeks because of overwhelming demand for trade in Halifax shares. Some customers had complained about being put on hold for up to 30 minutes. The company said the shutdowns for new customers were necessary in order to service existing clients. Rival stockbroker Yorkshare has also stopped marketing its services to new customers after being overloaded.
THE TIMES
-- UK 'HAS ROOM FOR MORE BIG STORES'

Research due out this week from retailing consultants Gmap is set to give supermarkets a boost. The report is expected to claim that large supermarket groups are no where near to saturating Britain, and that many places have room for more stores. Report author Martin Clarke also suggests that none of the big four groups is yet truly national in scope, and that local battles are likely as each seeks to acquire the remaining regional brands.
-- SHARP INCREASE IN NUMBER OF WOMEN EXECUTIVES IN UK

A survey by the Institute of Management has found that women are markedly increasing their presence in the UK's executive ranks, with the number of women managers increasing by 60 percent over the past four years. The research found that 15.2 percent of all Britain's executives are now women, and that one in three marketing managers and one in two personnel managers are women.
-- BECKETT READY TO REJECT BASS PROJECT

Bass is expected this week to finally hear the outcome of the Monopolies and Mergers Commission inquiry into its proposed takeover of rival brewer Carlsberg-Tetley. Speculation is rising that Trade Secretary Margaret Beckett will rule sometime this week, and that the deal will fall apart. It has been suggested that the MMC ruled that Bass would have to dispose of about half of its estate of tied and managed pubs if the deal were to proceed.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BRANSON GAINS NEW NOTES

Richard Branson's latest attempt to re-enter the music industry has received a 55 million stg boost from two former stockbrokers. Brothers Rory and Tim McCarthy paid the sum to acquire a 33 percent stake in Branson's new record label company V2. Branson is bidding to rejoin the music industry after a five-year interval. He was barred from the industry for 30 months after selling his Virgin Records to Thorn EMI in 1992.
-- CRIME ADDS 5.8 BILLION STG A YEAR TO SMALL FIRMS' COSTS

A survey published by the British Chambers of Commerce says crime costs Britain's small firms 5.8 billion stg a year. The report also says that while half of businesses in the sector have suffered theft, vandalism or arson, 85 percent of those surveyed expected to fall victim to crime. Respondents called for greater co-ordination between the corporate sector and the police, with 75 percent demanding a greater police presence.
-- SPACE SCIENTIST LANDS 12 MILLION STG FROM SHARES SALE

Bruce Smith, a computer scientist who worked on the first moon landing, has sold the company he founded to its senior management for 12 million stg. The company, Smith System Engineering, is a Surrey-based consultancy specialising in advanced computer technology. Employing 100 consultants, it advises commercial and government bodies on the use of satellite communications and supercomputers.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- JOSPIN ATTACKED OVER AEROSPATIALE PLANS

New French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has been warned that France could lose its place in the European aerospace industry if he abandons the plans of the previous government to privatise Aerospatiale. The warning has come from both British Aerospace, which is driving to consolidate Europe's fragmented aerospace and defence industries in face of rationalisation in the US, and from Dassault, the French warplane manufacturer.
-- PEER CALLS FOR DEPT OF WORK

Lord McCarthy, a Labour spokesman on employment in the House of Lords, is set to call for the setting up of a Department of Work and for more spending on vocational training. He will make his argument in a booklet published by the left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research. McCarthy claims that the new ministry is essential to help reduce unemployment, tackle skills shortages, improve industrial performance and enhance employees' rights.
-- GRID PENSIONERS TO LAUNCH NEW COURT CHALLENGE

Solicitors acting for two National Grid pensioners have said that last week's High Court ruling, which found that the Pensions Ombudsman had been wrong to side with the pensioners in a dispute with National Grid and National Power, could open the way for a wave of new complaints. The dispute relates to the way companies used pension fund surpluses to help finance redundancy programmes.
